**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I don’t know why I’m writing this. Maybe because the blank page feels like a dare, or maybe because I’ve always believed that if you stare into the void long enough, the void stares back—and sometimes, it hands you a pen. A thousand words is both nothing and everything. It’s the length of a decent short story, a rambling email to an old friend, a manifesto no one will read. It’s the space between two deep breaths.

I think about the words we don’t say more than the ones we do. The way a pause can strip a conversation bare, the way a glance can hold an entire argument. There’s a quiet violence in silence, but there’s also mercy. Some things shouldn’t be named. Some truths are too heavy for language.

Yesterday, I watched a spider in the corner of my ceiling. It wasn’t doing anything—just existing, suspended in its own small universe. I should have been repelled, but I envied it. No rent to pay, no emails to answer, no existential dread at 3 a.m. Just the patient wait for the next vibration in its web. Maybe that’s the secret: to stop struggling so hard to make meaning and just *be* a brief disturbance in the air.

I’ve been thinking about time lately. Not in the grand, philosophical sense—though that’s inevitable—but in the way it stretches and snaps like a rubber band. How an hour can crawl when you’re waiting for news, or disappear when you’re lost in a book. How a decade can feel like a lifetime ago or like it never happened at all. Memory is a liar. It smooths over the rough edges, turns villains into fools and fools into martyrs. We rewrite ourselves constantly, and by the end, we barely recognize the protagonist.

There’s a café I used to go to where the coffee tasted like nostalgia. The kind of place where the chairs were mismatched, the Wi-Fi was slow, and the barista remembered your order after one visit. It closed last year. I didn’t even notice until I walked past and saw the "For Lease" sign, the windows empty. It’s stupid how much that hurt. As if the absence of a building could take a piece of me with it. But places are just containers for moments, and moments are fragile. We carry them like glass orbs in our pockets, and one wrong step and they shatter.

I wonder if other people feel this way—like they’re both the main character and an extra in their own life. Some days, I’m the hero of my story: confident, witty, exactly where I’m supposed to be. Other days, I’m a background NPC in someone else’s cutscene, waiting for the camera to pan away so I can stop pretending. Maybe everyone is just improvising. Maybe we’re all just trying to look like we know what we’re doing.

I read once that the oldest known story is *The Epic of Gilgamesh*, and in it, the hero goes on a quest for immortality only to learn that the only thing that never dies is the story itself. That’s comforting in a way. We’re all temporary, but the words (the good ones, the true ones) linger. They get passed down, misquoted, tattooed on wrists, whispered in the dark. They outlive us.

But then, what’s the point of writing if no one reads it? And yet, here I am. Maybe the point isn’t the audience. Maybe it’s the act itself—the way the act of creation, even if it’s just for yourself, proves you were here. That you thought, you felt, you *tried*.

I’m at 500 words now. Halfway. The spider is still there, or maybe it’s a different one. Does it matter? The web is the same.

I think about the things I’ve lost: a childhood home, a grandparent’s voice, a version of myself that believed in easy answers. Grief isn’t just for people. It’s for the things that slip through your fingers no matter how tight you squeeze. But here’s the strange thing: the gaps where those things were aren’t empty. They’re full of light. Like when you hold your hand up to the sun and see the bones underneath—the absence is what lets the rest of you glow.

What else? Oh—the way rain sounds different depending on the surface it hits. The sizzle on hot pavement, the drumming on a tent, the soft *shhh* on grass. The way a song you haven’t heard in years can drop you into another time so suddenly you forget where you are. The way love, real love, isn’t a feeling so much as a decision: *I will keep choosing you, even when I don’t want to.*

I should probably wrap this up. A thousand words is a lot, but it’s also not enough. There’s always more to say. The trick is knowing when to stop.

So here’s my manifesto, my love letter, my eulogy for the unsaid:
We are brief. We are messy. We are doing our best. And sometimes, that’s enough.

(Word count: 1000 exactly. Or close enough.)
